heroIntro: Few experiences are as terrifying for a homeowner, developer, or commercial property owner as watching heavy municipal bulldozers and armed police detachments assemble outside your building at dawn. Development authorities such as the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (RAJUK), the Chattogram Development Authority (CDA), the Roads and Highways Department (RHD), or City Corporations frequently arrive to summarily demolish multi-story structures or seize private residential plots under the banner of 'unauthorized construction,' 'setback violation,' or 'government canal reclamation.' In countless instances, these administrative demolitions are executed in flagrant violation of statutory law: without serving mandatory statutory show-cause notices, without granting a personal hearing, or while illegally trespassing on legitimate private freehold land. In Bangladesh, no government agency is above the Constitution. Under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the High Court Division possesses extraordinary constitutional writ authority to issue emergency stay orders, halt bulldozers, and protect citizen properties from unlawful administrative destruction.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: How Can You Stop an Illegal Demolition or Eviction by RAJUK or Municipal Authorities in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: To halt an illegal demolition or eviction by statutory bodies like RAJUK, City Corporations, or the Roads and Highways Department, the aggrieved property owner must immediately file a Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. The petition argues that the administrative action violates statutory procedures (such as Section 3B of the Building Construction Act 1952) and infringes fundamental rights to property (Article 42) and equal protection of law (Articles 27 and 31). The High Court Division has the constitutional authority to issue an immediate ad-interim Stay Order or Direction of Status Quo, restraining authorities from demolishing, evicting, or altering the property until the legality of the administrative action is fully adjudicated.
highlights: Article 102 of the Constitution empowers the High Court to halt unlawful administrative demolitions immediately.
Demolition without serving a mandatory statutory show-cause notice violates fundamental principles of natural justice.
Building Construction Act 1952 mandates written notice and an opportunity to appeal to the Ministry of Housing.
High Court stay orders operate with immediate binding effect upon RAJUK, City Corporations, and executive magistrates.
points: Step 1: Secure all title deeds, approved building plans, layout approvals, mutation records, and tax receipts.
Step 2: Collect photographic and video proof of the municipal notices or physical demolition mobilization.
Step 3: Engage a Supreme Court advocate to draft an emergency Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution.
Step 4: Move the petition before the High Court Division's vacation or regular bench to secure an immediate Ad-Interim Stay Order.

sections.title: The Nightmare of Administrative Bulldozers in Urban Bangladesh
sections.content:
Across Dhaka and major urban conglomerates, private real estate investments face constant administrative exposure. Owners invest life savings, commercial loans, and years of effort into constructing commercial plazas, apartment buildings, or residential villas. However, during periodic administrative drives, teams from RAJUK, the Dhaka North or South City Corporation, the National River Conservation Commission, or the Roads and Highways Department suddenly target the property.

In many instances, field magistrates mark structures with red paint and declare them 'illegal encroachers' or cite minor deviations from building setback rules, threatening immediate demolition within 24 to 48 hours. Property owners are denied access to files, their approved architectural plans are disregarded, and local subordinate civil courts often express reluctance to issue injunctions against high-profile government drives. In this extreme emergency, the Constitution of Bangladesh provides the ultimate judicial sanctuary through the High Court Division.

sections.title: Statutory Provisions: Building Construction Act 1952
sections.content:
In Dhaka, construction approvals and regulatory compliance are governed by the Building Construction Act 1952 (East Bengal Act II of 1952) and the Dhaka Metropolitan Building Construction Rules (Dhaka Mohanogor Imarat Nirman Bidhimala). While these laws empower authorities to regulate urban sprawl, they strictly define procedural constraints.

Under Section 3B of the Building Construction Act 1952, where any construction has been commenced or completed in contravention of an approved plan or statutory rules, the authorized officer must first issue a written show-cause notice directing the owner to demolish or alter the construction within a reasonable period, or show cause why it should not be demolished. Crucially, Section 3C provides a statutory right of appeal to the Government (Ministry of Housing and Public Works) within thirty (30) days of receiving an adverse order. Any demolition executed before this appeal window expires, or without serving written notice, is ultra vires (beyond legal powers) and legally void.

If municipal or development action crosses over into formal state taking of private land, review Acquisition Act 2017 Section 4 notice and 200%–300% compensation rules before accepting any Deputy Commissioner assessment.

sections.title: The Principle of Natural Justice: Mandatory Show-Cause Notice
sections.content:
The foundational bedrock of administrative law in Bangladesh is the universal principle of natural justice, codified under the Latin maxim Audi alteram partem (no person shall be condemned unheard). The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly laid down that any administrative action that deprives a citizen of property, livelihood, or shelter without prior notice and a meaningful hearing is arbitrary and void.

Development authorities frequently bypass this constitutional safeguard by executing 'mobile court drives' or posting notices on outer gates hours before demolition. When an advocate challenges this behavior before the High Court, demonstrating that no personal notice was served and no opportunity to produce approved plans was afforded, the High Court invalidates the administrative action. Arbitrary administrative speed cannot override constitutional fairness.

sections.title: Article 102: Constitutional Writ Powers of the High Court
sections.content:
When state functionaries or statutory corporations violate statutory procedures and threaten citizen properties, the aggrieved person has the constitutional right to invoke Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh before the High Court Division.

Under Article 102(1) and 102(2)(a)(ii), the High Court Division may make an order declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. A Writ of Mandamus or Certiorari can be sought to compel the authority to act strictly within the four corners of the statute, to quash arbitrary demolition notices, and to protect the citizen's fundamental rights under Article 31 (protection of law), Article 32 (protection of life and liberty), and Article 42 (right to property).

sections.title: Securing an Emergency Ad-Interim Stay Order
sections.content:
When bulldozers are on the move, property owners do not have months or even weeks to litigate. The primary strategic objective of filing an Article 102 Writ Petition is securing an immediate, emergency Ad-Interim Order of Stay or Direction of Status Quo.

A skilled Supreme Court advocate drafts the writ petition with extreme urgency, annexing all approved plans, municipal tax receipts, title deeds, and photographic evidence of the threatened demolition. The advocate mentions the matter before the appropriate Division Bench of the High Court. Upon demonstrating a prima facie case of administrative illegality and the imminent threat of irreparable destruction, the High Court issues a Rule Nisi against RAJUK, the Ministry of Housing, and municipal authorities, and grants an immediate interim stay restraining all demolition or eviction for a period of three to six months. This order is communicated immediately via official court copy and advocate notice to the executive magistrate, instantly halting the bulldozers.

sections.title: Approved Plan Deviations and Compounding Regulations
sections.content:
In reality, many urban buildings contain minor structural deviations from their originally approved architectural plans: an extended cantilever balcony, a slight encroachment into a side setback, or a rooftop shade. RAJUK often cites these minor deviations to justify demolishing entire multi-story buildings.

The law in Bangladesh distinguishes between complete unauthorized construction (building without any plan) and minor plan deviations. Under the Imarat Nirman Bidhimala, minor setback or floor area ratio (FAR) deviations that do not endanger structural stability or public safety are subject to 'compounding'—meaning the regulatory authority can impose statutory penalty fines and approve revised as-built plans. In writ proceedings, the High Court frequently restrains demolition and directs RAJUK to examine the owner's compounding application within a specified timeframe, protecting the multi-crore investment from wrecking balls.

sections.title: Land Acquisition Act 2017 vs. Unlawful Road Eviction
sections.content:
Another widespread form of administrative predation involves the Roads and Highways Department (RHD), City Corporations, or Railway authorities widening roads or digging canals through private freehold land without formal acquisition. Government agencies frequently claim the private land is 'vested property' or part of an old historical road alignment.

Under Article 42 of the Constitution and the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act 2017, the state cannot seize an inch of private land without initiating formal Section 4 acquisition notices, hearing joint verification objections, and paying statutory compensation (which stands at 200% for public acquisitions and 300% for non-governmental projects). If municipal authorities attempt to bulldoze boundary walls or seize private land without gazetted acquisition and compensation, the High Court will issue a writ prohibiting eviction and commanding the state to pay full statutory compensation before any possession is taken.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Stopping a RAJUK Demolition in Uttara
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) illustrates how an emergency High Court writ saved a commercial building in Uttara, Dhaka:

An expatriate businessman constructed a 6-story commercial building in Sector 11, Uttara, backed by an approved RAJUK architectural plan obtained in 2021. In late 2024, a newly appointed RAJUK zone magistrate, conducting a canal cleaning drive, marked the rear 15 feet of the building with red paint, claiming it violated canal setback regulations. The magistrate refused to inspect the owner's approved plan or mutation documents, verbally announcing that bulldozers would demolish the rear portion of the building on the following Sunday morning.

The owner retained a Supreme Court constitutional writ advocate on Thursday afternoon. Working overnight, the advocate compiled a comprehensive dossier: the original RAJUK approval letters, CS and RS Khatian maps showing the property was situated on private freehold land separate from the canal, and photographs of the red markings. On Friday and Saturday, the advocate drafted an emergency Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution, citing violation of Section 3B of the Building Construction Act 1952 and fundamental rights under Articles 27, 31, and 42.

On Sunday morning, the advocate moved the matter before the High Court Division bench upon urgent mention. The High Court Bench immediately issued a Rule Nisi and passed an ad-interim Stay Order restraining RAJUK and the executive magistrate from demolishing or entering the property for six months. The advocate served the certified operative order to the RAJUK chairman and executive magistrate by 11:30 AM, just as the demolition crew arrived on site. The magistrate halted the operation immediately. Later, during the rule hearing, RAJUK admitted that the private plot had been confused with an adjacent government parcel, and the demolition threat was permanently vacated, saving an investment valued at BDT 12,00,00,000.

faqs.question: Can RAJUK demolish a building without giving notice in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. Under Section 3B of the Building Construction Act 1952 and the universal principles of natural justice, RAJUK is legally required to serve a formal written show-cause notice granting the property owner reasonable time to respond before initiating any demolition.

faqs.question: What is an Article 102 Writ Petition in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: An Article 102 Writ Petition is a constitutional lawsuit filed directly before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh to challenge illegal, arbitrary, or unconstitutional actions taken by government authorities, statutory bodies, or executive magistrates.

faqs.question: How fast can I get a stay order from the High Court to stop a bulldozer?
faqs.answer: In genuine emergencies where demolition is imminent, a Supreme Court advocate can draft and move an emergency writ petition before the High Court Division within 24 to 48 hours to secure an immediate ad-interim stay order.

faqs.question: What happens if RAJUK ignores a High Court stay order and continues demolition?
faqs.answer: Disobeying a High Court stay order constitutes criminal Contempt of Court under the Contempt of Courts Act 1926. The High Court can summon the offending magistrates and officials in person, impose prison sentences, and order the government to pay full compensation for any damage.

faqs.question: Can minor deviations from an approved building plan be legalized (compounded)?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under the Dhaka Metropolitan Building Construction Rules, minor setback or floor area deviations that do not threaten structural safety can be regularized upon payment of statutory compounding penalty fees to RAJUK.

faqs.question: Can the government seize private land for road widening without compensation?
faqs.answer: No. Under Article 42 of the Constitution and the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act 2017, the government must issue formal acquisition notices and pay statutory compensation (200% to 300% of market value) before taking private land.

faqs.question: What documents do I need to file an emergency writ petition against RAJUK?
faqs.answer: You need certified title deeds, Khatian records, approved building architectural plans, mutation documents, tax receipts (Dakhila), any written municipal notices, and photographs or video proof of the threatened demolition.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi (NRB) file a writ petition from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. An NRB property owner can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh High Commission or Embassy abroad, appointing a representative or advocate in Bangladesh to institute and argue the writ petition in the High Court.
